title: 97% of the art is machine-generated, and the 3% that isn't is cats
_drafted: 2026-08-19 by the pdoom1-website seat, from Pip's own email the same evening. His reasoning is preserved verbatim below because the copy is downstream of it.
_why_this_campaign_exists: The standing criticism of p(Doom)1 is that the art looks AI-generated. It does, and on 2026-08-19 a working artist confirmed it within minutes of opening the asset pack. Pip's answer has always been a promise ('the funding is for human artists'). This campaign replaces the promise with a MEASURED NUMBER that a script re-derives: 97.0% of packed art is model-generated, and the only part that is not is contributed cat photos. Publishing the baseline is what makes any future movement legible, and it is strictly harder to fake than a promise.
_pips_reasoning_verbatim: Game is complex engine and mechanics
If I make game look good with poo mechanics, game fails
therefore I want to make barely playable game and mostly focus on mechanics
turns out humans want good art and UI and UX, they've gotten greedy, the bastards
Spending 200 hours making up some concept art and placeholder images is much bad use of my time compared to 200 dev hours
People need to be able to get at least the theme and gist of what I am talking about
the nature of the game still is open to a lot of artistic choices, eg how detailed, what camera angles, how isometric, what button styles, what icon styles, what ui elements change over time
This needs us to cohere on some artistic themes, but I don't want to lock in too early
Obviously badly made AI art is bad, and steals from artists
Paying you to make 200 sample images or little sprites for the office if I then go change the camera angle is silly, and I don't have any money (yet)
Paying you to make high quality art of things we are highly likely to keep, i.e. stills of poster images, key animations, hero animations, etc, seems useful because that's where highest quality lies
Paying for tokens to do some things seems like a reasonable intermediate step, especially as this game is about the dangers of ratcheting capabilities
I'd rather get image generation done from e.g. some model that has been ethically trained on things that people opt into, rather than functionally stolen art
I would rather not get slowed down too much by the above point, we only have so many days before AGI

copy.manifund_update:
**Where the art actually stands, as a number rather than a promise**

The honest criticism of this project is that the art looks AI-generated. It does. So rather than promise to fix it, here is the measurement, taken today and reproducible from the repo:

- **97.0%** of packed art is model-generated (488 of 503 files)
- **2.6%** is not: eight photographs of contributors' cats, and five hand-written SVGs of the same cats
- **0.4%** is unattributable, and is recorded as `unknown` rather than guessed
- **0%** of the soundtrack is generated -- all eight tracks are captures of hand-authored patches, judged by ear

That 97% is not an estimate. Every packed asset now carries a provenance record naming what produced it and what evidence says so, and a guard refuses the commit if the manifest and the shipped assets disagree, or if a new unattributable asset appears. Six files were unattributable when this started; four were resolved by reading signed credentials embedded in the files themselves, and two remain, pinned by content hash so they cannot be quietly forgotten.

The grant commitment is "human artists to replace current AI-generated assets". Until today that was a sentence. It is now a number with a denominator, and the mechanism that notices the first time it moves is already running: the moment one non-cat, non-generated art asset ships, the check announces it in the build output.

**Why the art is generated in the first place**, stated plainly: the hard part of this game is the simulation, and 200 hours spent drawing placeholders is 200 hours not spent on mechanics. The art direction is also genuinely unsettled -- camera angle, detail level, how isometric it should be, which UI elements change as doom rises -- and commissioning hundreds of sprites before those are decided would waste an artist's time and money I do not yet have. Generated art is a fast way to find out what I actually want, and the finding-out happens by throwing most of it away: on 14 August I judged 470 assets in 23 minutes and discarded 274 of them.

Where paid work goes first, when there is money: the things most likely to survive a change of direction -- poster stills, key animations, hero frames. Highest quality where quality lasts longest.

One preference stated without over-claiming: where generation is used, I would rather use models trained on opted-in work than on scraped work, and I am not going to pretend the current pack meets that bar.

The number is 97%. It moves when someone gets paid.
copy.devlog_long:
# 97%

I counted. It is 97.0% -- 488 of 503 packed art files are machine-generated.

I had guessed that number in an email this morning, before anything measured it. That is either good instincts or the kind of coincidence that should make a person go and check the arithmetic. The arithmetic checks.

## The 3% is cats

Eight photographs of contributors' cats, and five hand-drawn SVGs of the same cats. That is the entire non-generated portion of the art. Take the cats out and packed art is 99.6% generated.

The cats are there because people sent them, with permission, and the game picks one at random per run so every one of them reaches players. The only part of the visual layer a person made on purpose is a cat.

## The soundtrack is 0%

All eight audio files are recorded as `procedural_render`: captures of hand-authored patches, composed by ear over the workshop sessions with an LLM as the live-coding instrument. A naive human-or-AI field was rejected during design precisely because these are neither, in the naive sense. I have not been saying this out loud, and I should have been.

## Why a number and not a promise

The standing answer to "your art looks AI-generated" has been "the funding is for human artists". That is a promise, and promises are unfalsifiable right up until they are broken.

So every packed asset now carries a provenance record: what produced it, and what evidence establishes that. Six were genuinely unattributable when the pass started. Four were resolved by reading signed credentials that were inside the files the whole time. Two remain, recorded as `unknown` and pinned by content hash -- pinned, because a mechanism that forces the question later is worth more than a document that asks nicely.

A guard now refuses the commit if the manifest and the shipped pack disagree, if an asset arrives with no record, or if the unknown set changes in either direction. It shipped on 11 August wired to nothing, which is how an asset slipped in on the 12th with no record at all and went unnoticed for a week. That is fixed too, and the fix is the more useful half of the story: a mechanism nobody runs is a document.

## What the number is for

It is a baseline. It moves when someone is paid to move it, and not otherwise. When it moves I will say by how much, from what to what, and what the money bought.

p(Doom)1 is a game about the people trying to stop AI going badly wrong. You cannot win; you can only buy time.

[Play it](https://pdoom1.com/?utm_source=devlog&utm_medium=owned&utm_campaign=97-percent-2026-08) - [back it](https://manifund.org/projects/fund-development-of-pdoom1)
